display: Third-generation knife sharpener in Sakai, Osaka. I sharpen and repair Japanese kitchen knives by hand, take mail-in knives from overseas, and attend trade fairs in Asia.

signals.text: I'm going to a hotel and restaurant equipment fair in Asia this autumn and want chefs to see a live edge on a Japanese knife.
I'll be at the Shanghai hotel and restaurant equipment fair, November 18–21, booth B214 in the middle row, sharpening live samples on a folding bench.
I keep redoing the numbers for the Shanghai trip. Booth, flights, hotel and shipping the bench add up to more than I made at the last fair, and I'm afraid it will lose money.
I don't want to be a salesman. I want buyers to see the edge and judge the work themselves, and I need a way to show it that doesn't feel like pitching.
I want to know what restaurant buyers in China actually want before deciding whether fairs are worth the cost.
I'd like a Mandarin speaker I can trust to help me talk with visitors at the booth. My English is slow and my Chinese is nonexistent.
Overseas parcels keep arriving badly packed, sometimes a bare blade in a thin envelope, and customs forms cause delays. I'm looking for a better way to handle this.
Overseas customers keep asking for engraving, and I'd like to add it as a paid extra.
A fourteen-year-old in my neighbourhood wants to learn sharpening, and I'm thinking about how to teach a beginner properly.
After decades of leaning over the stones my body is tired, and I'm looking for ways to keep working with less strain.
I'd like to find buyers who value careful hand sharpening, since I can't win on price against cheap factory knives.
I'm worried about the shop's long-term income and lean on overseas mail-in work to keep it steady.

offers.text: Hand sharpening and restoration of Japanese kitchen knives (yanagiba, deba, usuba, santoku) on whetstones from 1000 to 8000 grit plus natural Aoto.
Repairs: re-handling, rust removal, chip repair, and re-grinding warped blades.
A mail-in service for overseas customers with a free padded sleeve. Turnaround is two weeks, and I don't rush an edge.
A family shop in Sakai with a bench for four people, two water-cooled grinders and a small display counter.
Thirty-two years of customer notebooks recording each knife, its steel and what the owner wanted. This is practical knowledge about how knives age and how people use them.
A live sharpening demonstration at trade fairs, with a folding bench, sample knives and leaflets in simplified Chinese.
Advice for home cooks and chefs on hand washing, stones and edge care, and on what rust removal will and won't restore.
Willing to teach the basics of sharpening to a curious beginner, starting by watching at the bench.
Some experience with fairs in Bangkok and Shanghai and with how Asian restaurant buyers respond to craft knives. I can share what I've seen.

catchers.hypo: I run a restaurant in Singapore, and my chefs' knives are dull and chipped. Can you take regular batches by mail and sharpen them?
catchers.can: Take a batch by mail through the English website and sharpen each knife by hand in about two weeks. My son handles bookings and payment.
catchers.confirm: Are your knives Japanese-style single-bevel or double-bevel kitchen knives that can be posted in padded packaging?

catchers.hypo: My father's old yanagiba is rusty and I can't bear to throw it away. Can it be saved?
catchers.can: Remove the rust and restore the edge. The finish will change slightly, and I treat each knife as if it were my own.
catchers.confirm: Are you happy with a restored blade whose finish looks slightly different from the original?

catchers.hypo: I'm a buyer for a restaurant group in Shanghai. Would you let our head chef try your edge in person at the fair?
catchers.can: Sharpen sample knives live at booth B214, talk through the work, and take the chef's own knife.
catchers.confirm: Are you interested in hand-sharpened Japanese knives, rather than only buying new knives?

catchers.hypo: I speak Mandarin and English and I'm in Shanghai in November. Do you need someone to help you at your booth?
catchers.can: Tell them exactly which days I need help, and what I can cover within a tight budget.
catchers.confirm: Can you be at the Shanghai fair between November 18 and 21 and do you understand knives well enough to explain a sharpening demo?

catchers.hypo: I run a small business that ships fragile goods between Japan and other countries. Can I help with your customs forms and packaging?
catchers.can: Compare my current routine with theirs and use whatever makes parcels and customs forms simpler.
catchers.confirm: Do you have hands-on experience with customs paperwork and packing for blades or other sharp metal goods?

catchers.hypo: Our tea class has a few pairs of scissors that are dull. Can you sharpen them?
catchers.can: Through my wife's tea class in Sakai, I sharpen scissors for the students. The first pair is free.
catchers.confirm: Are the scissors something that can be dropped off in Sakai, rather than shipped from overseas?

catchers.hypo: My teenager is curious about traditional crafts. Could they come and watch you work?
catchers.can: Invite the young person to watch first at the shop on a Saturday. A neighbour's grandson who may start an apprenticeship next spring is in the same position.
catchers.confirm: Is the young person nearby, and willing to start by just watching for a few visits?

catchers.hypo: I'm a craftsperson in a similar trade and I'm planning my first overseas fair. How do you decide whether it will pay?
catchers.can: Share my own numbers and worries about the Bangkok and Shanghai fairs. Mr. Sugiura, an old friend in the guild, knows many fair stories and can add his own.
catchers.confirm: Is this a hand craft that sells on the quality of the work rather than on the price?

forbids.text: I will not rush an edge, so I don't take jobs that need one.
I don't want to compete with cheap factory knives on price.
I can't be away from the shop for more than ten days in a row, because my regular restaurants need their knives.
I won't borrow money for the trip.
I won't promise a turnaround shorter than two weeks.
I'm not a salesman, and I won't do pushy selling.

projects.name: Shanghai fair booth, November 18–21
projects.text: A live sharpening booth at a hotel and restaurant equipment fair, with a folding bench, sample knives, and leaflets in simplified Chinese. The aim is to show the edge to buyers and cover the trip's cost.
roles_needed: Restaurant buyer or chef who can try an edge
Local guide for logistics in Shanghai
Shipper or courier for the folding bench

projects.name: Overseas mail-in service
projects.text: About fifteen parcels a month from the US, Australia and Singapore. We want better packing, simpler customs handling, and a paid engraving option.

policy.t1: When there is a real sign of a fit, I'll share the fair dates, booth details, how many parcels I get a month, and my worries about whether the trip will pay.
policy.t2: Once trust is established, I'll share the real revenue picture, my physical condition, and my son's offer to share costs.
policy.never: My exact income, medical records, and the names of my regular restaurants.
